newsitem.title: USA: Skepticism about government on Gulf War illness.
newsitem.headline: Skepticism about government on Gulf War illness.

text.p: The Pentagon, under fire for its handling of the mysterious illnesses affecting thousands of veterans of the Gulf War, said on Wednesday it would ask for help from the prestigious National Academy of Sciences.

Deputy Defence Secretary John White told a meeting of the Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans' Illnesses that he has asked the National Academy of Sciences to convene an expert committee to advise the Pentagon and recommend changes in its programmes.
He was trying to head off adoption by the panel of a staff recommendation to remove research into the illnesses entirely from the Defence Department and turn it over to someone else.

Members of the committee, which must make its recommendations to President Bill Clinton by the end of the year, were openly sceptical about the government's findings and the slow pace of tracing events five years ago, which may provide clues to the illnesses. "There is a perceptual problem, even perception of a cover-up," complained Elaine Larson, a Georgetown University dean.

Asked if it was possible the Defence Department and the Central Intelligence Agency acted to cover up evidence of chemical munitions explosions in southern Iraq that may have caused some of the illnesses, White replied: "Could be, yes."
He said investigators were looking into the possibility that someone may have withheld information.

CIA Executive Director Nora Slatkin told the committee it was not until September of 1995 that the agency identified a chemical weapons storage bunker and pit at Khamisiyah as a site where chemical weapons may have been released when U.S. troops detonated some weapons.

But committee members said they were frustrated that the Pentagon and CIA cannot even decide what day in 1991 the explosions took place, critical information in determining who may have been affected because of weather and wind conditions.

They also were troubled by Slatkin's responses to questions about evidence and hearsay that Iraqi forces may have fired some chemical weapons. Slatkin said that while the CIA did not doubt that chemical weapons alarms went off and a Czech monitoring team had evidence of chemical weapons use, "we continue to conclude that Iraq did not use chemical or biological weapons during the Gulf War."
Larson called it "a very crafted, limited statement" and added that "it causes a high level of mistrust."

The Pentagon on Tuesday said it was increasing from 12 to 110 the number of people investigating the causes of the illnesses and was contacting some 20,000 U.S. Gulf War veterans who may have been within a 30 mile (50 km) radius of Khamisiyah.

The Pentagon has denied any coverup of possible exposure of U.S. troops to Iraqi chemical weapons in the 1991 Gulf War, saying there was no evidence of U.S. deaths or injuries from chemical agents or of Iraqi use of them against U.S. forces.
Veterans groups plan to petition Attorney General Janet Reno to appoint an independent counsel to investigate the government's evidence of chemical weapons exposure.
